column4: In the same Lot episode as 54:38, a stone storm is sent against the people while Lot's family is saved before dawn; it adds the concrete attack and dawn rescue behind the cited morning punishment.
The people press Lot for access to his guests and are blinded; this is a specific mob assault on protected visitors, echoing the source's secondary th-w-r sense of people leaping upon a target.

On the Day of Resurrection a person asks where escape is; this directly matches the section's claim that the charge into the crowd marks the moment with nowhere left to flee, and its explicit turn toward the final day.
The answer to the escape question in 75:10 is that there is no refuge; this verse supplies the inescapability that the section makes central to its dawn-strike image.

Continuing the fighting rules near 2:190, it says that if opponents cease there is to be no aggression (عُدْوَانَ) except against wrongdoers; this gives the section's ʿudwān root a precise boundary in a combat context.
God permits kindness and justice toward people who have not fought the believers or driven them from home; this limits the section's enemy/friend distinction by the actual conduct of the other party.
The next verse forbids taking as allies those who fought, expelled, or aided expulsion; it identifies the concrete hostile conduct that distinguishes an enemy from those addressed in 60:8.
This completes the Lot destruction begun in 11:82 by identifying its marked stones and saying the punishment is not far from wrongdoers; it adds the judgment's specific target and warning.
This follows the morning cry in 15:83 by saying that the people of al-Hijr's earnings did not avail them; it states that resources could not protect the struck community.

At Uhud, the fighting group falters and divides between desire for this world and the Hereafter; this is a battle-context counterpoint to the section's link from a cavalry charge and spoils to intense attachment to worldly “good.”

The people of the fortified houses think their strongholds will protect them, yet removal comes unexpectedly and terror is cast into their hearts; this is a specific reversal of the section's unprepared encampment, with confidence in defenses replacing sleep.

Garden owners swear to go early and harvest, but the overnight calamity in the surrounding passage ruins their plan; this is a specific dawn-going reversal of the section's successful dawn assault, though it is a harvest rather than combat.

They explicitly plan to keep a poor person out of the garden; this is a specific but indirect boundary on the source's booty-sharing detail, since the verse concerns hoarded produce rather than war spoils.

One member described as the group's “middle” or most judicious person rebukes the others after their loss; the root w-s-ṭ shifts from the source's physical center of a crowd to a moral voice within a group.

The source's w-s-ṭ describes cavalry entering the physical center of a gathered crowd; this verse uses the same root for a community characterized as balanced and just, an indirect contrast between occupying a group's center and serving as its ethical middle.
